summary: Reports on an IETF workshop held at MIT on 28 May 2008, organized by the area directors for real-time applications and infrastructure. It discussed delay and congestion problems caused by growing peer-to-peer traffic. It is an informational workshop report, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo reports a workshop held by the IETF to look at the congestion caused by peer-to-peer traffic. It records what providers and application developers described, the fixes that were discussed, and the short list of items people wanted to work on afterwards.

questions: how to reduce p2p network congestion
subtitle: What an IETF workshop on peer-to-peer traffic concluded, and what it left to do.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer file sharing pushes large volumes of delay-tolerant traffic onto links shared with everything else, and at peak times the whole link fills up, so interactive traffic waits.
tldr.mechanism: The workshop collected what providers and application developers saw, and worked through possible fixes: helping peers choose closer peers, making bulk transfers yield to interactive traffic, and using service classes.
tldr.outcome: Two transport work items and one peer-selection work item gained the most interest: a deferential end-to-end congestion control for bulk transfers, an informational document on applications opening many connections, and work on information sharing for peer selection.

today: RFC 5594 is an Informational memo published in July 2009, reporting a workshop held on 28 May 2008 at MIT. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a report of a discussion rather than a specification, and it ends with a list of candidate work items.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Large internet service providers were increasingly running into trouble with peer-to-peer traffic. Transferring static, delay-tolerant data between nodes is a well understood problem, but traditional management of fairness at the transport layer is under strain from applications designed to reach the best end-user transfer rates. At peak times networks run near absolute capacity, so all traffic incurs delay, and the applications that suffer most are the real-time ones such as Voice over IP and internet gaming.

The Real-time Applications and Infrastructure area directors organised a workshop on peer-to-peer infrastructure and invited contributions from people working in the problem and solution spaces. The goals were twofold: to understand the technical problems that providers and end users were experiencing as a result of high volumes of peer-to-peer traffic, and to begin to understand how the IETF might be helpful. Finding out where in the IETF the work might be pursued, and how to extract feasible work items, were treated as important tasks. The focus was on engineering solutions that promised some imminent benefit to the Internet as a whole, rather than longer-term research or closed proprietary solutions. Public policy must inform the work, but crafting or debating policy was outside the scope.

Position papers were solicited in the weeks before the workshop and a limited number of speakers were invited to present. The report summarises all the contributions. The workshop showed the IETF community's recognition of the effect of peer-to-peer and other high-volume applications on the Internet as a whole, and participants welcomed the chance to discuss standardisation work that operators, application providers and end users would all find useful. Two transport-related work items gained significant traction: designing a protocol for very deferential end-to-end congestion control for delay-tolerant applications, and producing an informational document about the reasoning behind and the effects of applications opening multiple transport connections at once. A separate area of interest focused on improving peer selection by having networks make more information available to applications. Presenters also covered traditional approaches to multiple service-tier queuing such as Diffserv.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop asked two questions: what is actually going wrong, and what could the IETF usefully do about it. It answers the first with reports from a cable provider and from a file-sharing developer, and the second with a list of possible work items.

sections.title: Scoping the Problem
sections.content:
The workshop grew out of the pain points large providers were experiencing with high volumes of peer-to-peer traffic, but several participants felt the IETF should approach a more general space of problems, of which peer-to-peer congestion may be only one instance. High-volume applications other than peer-to-peer, whether they already exist or have yet to be developed, could cause similar congestion. The general class of congestion problems attributable to always-on, high-volume applications needs solutions that are reasonable for operators, applications and subscribers at once.

Although most attention has been paid to congestion on access links, increased traffic volumes could affect other parts of the network. Although the workshop focused on the causes and effects of current peer-to-peer traffic volumes, the document says it will likely be useful in future for the IETF to consider how to pursue solutions to these larger problems.

The document also suggests that obtaining more data about internet congestion may be a helpful step before solutions are pursued, focusing on where in the network congestion occurs, how long it lasts and how often it happens, what its effects are and what its root causes are. Individual providers expressed interest in sharing congestion data, but strategies for reliably and regularly obtaining and disseminating such data on a broad scale remain elusive.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop's message to the IETF was that peer-to-peer traffic is one example of a wider problem: any application that runs all day and moves a lot of data can fill a shared link and slow everything else down.

sections.title: The Service Provider's View
sections.content:
Two presenters gave the workshop the view of a network operator. The first described the cable network architecture used in many cable systems. A single cable modem termination system may serve hundreds or thousands of residential customers, and each has several DOCSIS domains, typically with one downstream link and a number of upstream links. The limiting resource is usually bandwidth, and congestion shows up when instantaneous load exceeds capacity.

In the upstream direction, any modem connected to the termination system can ask to transmit, and requests are randomised to reduce collisions. With many modems asking at once, requests collide and delays appear. DOCSIS does not specify a buffer size for modems, but buffer delays of one to four seconds have been observed with modems from different vendors. Once the termination system has granted a modem permission to send, that modem can piggyback its next request on the data it sends. With a lot of upstream traffic, piggybacking happens more often, and that sends heavy upstream users to the front of the queue, ahead of interactive but less upstream-intensive applications. If requests are granted about every one to three milliseconds, a modem carrying voice traffic with a packetisation delay of 20 to 30 milliseconds can end up in contention with a modem that transmits constantly and piggybacks every request. The presenters said this may explain how heavy upstream users dominate the pipe, and that assessments of the problem should keep the influence of the specific layer 2 network in mind.

How TCP flow fairness applies to those upstream requests is an open question. The termination system sees many service flows, each of which could be a single TCP flow or many TCP flows or UDP traffic, and it does not know the source or destination IP address of a packet until it has already been sent upstream, so those cannot be used to impose flow fairness. A modem can have several service flows defined; a modem that is also a voice endpoint can provision a service flow for voice traffic that avoids the upstream request process and its contention, with upstream capacity provisioned for it, alongside a separate best-efforts flow. Some providers provision such a flow for their own voice offering, and others let subscribers pay for it. A provider may also provision one on the fly when it recognises the need, classifying flows with Diffserv bits set by the customer premises equipment.

The second part described what cable providers were doing. In 2005, customers began complaining more about the performance of delay-sensitive traffic, and providers saw heavy growth in peer-to-peer traffic and a growing correlation between high peer-to-peer activity and packet loss. The newest generation of the DOCSIS specification enables faster transfer rates than most systems support, but the presenters said this would likely not remove the need for congestion management while client software is designed to consume bandwidth regardless of available capacity.

The response being trialled was protocol-agnostic. All traffic used to be marked best efforts; during the trials it is reclassified as priority. When a termination system approaches peak congestion on a port, some subscribers have their traffic reclassified as best efforts again, using a new default service flow with the same provisioned bandwidth as the priority stream but lower priority. Which subscribers are re-marked is decided by whether they have entered a long duration bulk consumption state, measured by how much bandwidth they use over how many minutes, with thresholds that depend on the service tier so that subscribers who pay for more bandwidth get higher ones. The re-marking does not distinguish between several users of the same connection, so one family member's peer-to-peer use can lower another family member's web traffic, and there is no mechanism for users to find out that their traffic has been re-marked. The aim is to preserve a good experience for subscribers with bursty traffic, including real-time applications; compared with reducing a subscriber's bandwidth outright, this keeps applications from setting their own priority levels, but it avoids the connotations some users attach to bandwidth reductions.
sections.plainLanguage: A cable network sends data upstream through a shared queue that modems take turns to enter. A modem that is sending a lot of data gets to ask for the queue more often, so it can push ahead of a modem carrying a live voice call. The provider's trial re-marks heavy users' traffic as best efforts when the port is close to full.

sections.title: Improving Peer Selection
sections.content:
How peers are selected is an integral factor in the efficiency of peer-to-peer networks, for both the provider and the client. The way clients select peers varies between protocols and clients, but in general peers are largely oblivious to routing and topology information, which produces topologies that ignore the network underneath. Approaches to closing the gap involve an entity that knows the network, such as a provider, making some of that information available to clients or trackers, so that traffic can be localised or peer selection altered.

Any change to peer selection has engineering trade-offs. BitTorrent used randomised peer selection by design: choosing peers at random from a large selection averages out problems among peers and allows connections to good peers that may be far away. It also supports rarest-first piece selection, which lets a swarm continue when the original seed disappears and spreads pieces so that more peers hold something others want. Any move away from random selection has to take these factors into account. The incentives on both sides are also complex: a provider may want to move traffic off its own network and so hand over information with the opposite effect from what peers expect, while peers will only consult the network if the information improves their performance.

Five approaches were described. Using autonomous system numbers, a peer could prefer peers in its own autonomous system. Transfers inside one autonomous system may be faster on some networks. On mobile networks the usefulness is limited, because autonomous system numbers do not correspond to geography. A case study with the four most popular BitTorrent torrents found swarm sizes of 9984, 3944, 2561 and 2023, with size distributions appearing to be polynomial. Where a swarm had more than 20 peers in one autonomous system, those peers could trade only with each other and avoid interdomain traffic, and more than half of the peers in the four swarms were in autonomous systems of that size, so connecting inside one autonomous system could reduce transit traffic by at least 57%. With asymmetric links the user experience may worsen, because a peer's download speed would be limited by the slower upload speed. With the largest swarm at 9984, the chance of two peers sharing a neighbourhood is too low for locality below the autonomous system to be worth pursuing.

The Provider Portal for Peer-to-Peer Applications project lets providers and applications cooperate, with providers including internet service providers, content distribution networks and caching services. Each provider can reach peer-to-peer clients through a portal called an iTracker, identified by a DNS SRV record, a whois lookup or a trusted third party. An iTracker expresses the virtual cost of the provider's internal and external links, which may reflect any provider preference and may be based on utilisation, transit costs or geography. In a test with two parallel swarms of similar size and distribution sharing the same file, one using the framework with the provider's network topology map fed to its iTracker and one using traditional peer selection, the swarm without the framework saw 98% of its traffic to and from peers outside the provider, against 50% with it, and download completion times improved by about 20% on average.

A multi-layer tracker architecture adds local trackers that give the same information as the global tracker but only for content inside their own local scope, with client queries redirected from the global tracker to the right local tracker, and further redirection when local trackers exist at several levels. The hard question is what local means for trackers, seeds and peers, since locality could depend on traffic conditions, load balancing, static topology or policy. Finding the right local tracker can be done off-path, with local trackers registering in advance, or on-path, with the network proxying requests; the off-path approach is preferable for performance and reliability. Providers may also be concerned about legal liability in helping peers find unauthorised copies.

An ISP-aided neighbour selection service would put an oracle on the provider's network. The oracle receives a list of IP addresses from a network node, sorts the list by its own confidential criteria and returns it, which could be seen as a special case of the virtual cost interface. It could be run as a web server or a UDP service at a known location. For interdomain ranking the provider could put its own peers first or rank on autonomous system number, and providers could have their oracles exchange lists. The main difficulty is scale: if every peer sends the addresses of every peer it knows, requests become very large, and the largest swarms already approach 10000 peers. Letting trackers issue the requests, or using other peers' sorted lists as input, would reduce the volume. The approach also has the advantage of not requiring providers to know where particular content might be located or to have any role in directing peers to it.

Caches were suggested as peers in peer-to-peer networks. They could ease network load by reducing the need for peers to upload to each other and by localising traffic. For caches to be useful they would likely need to be large: one suggestion was that a 1 TB cache could serve 30% of requests within a single autonomous system and a 100 TB cache could serve 80%. Large caches need sizeable bandwidth to avoid contention among peers, and would not be usefully placed inside a hybrid fibre-coaxial network on a cable system. The legal liability of hosting a cache probably reduces the incentive to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers a client picks decide how much traffic crosses the Internet. Several ideas were on the table: tell clients which network a peer is in, let the provider publish the cost of its own links, add trackers that know only about local copies, and let the provider rank the peers it hears about.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Quality of Service
sections.content:
A survey presented at the workshop found that providers see traffic volumes from heavy users as a problem, but that no single congestion management tool has been put to wide use. In the developer and research communities, congestion caused by peer-to-peer traffic has spurred new thinking about congestion control at both the transport layer and the application layer.

On end-to-end congestion control, the observation was that the uptake of peer-to-peer use can produce perceptible latency of the order of seconds for interactive applications. A user with an uplink of 250 to 500 Kbps and a modem buffer of 32 to 64 Kbps can easily fill that buffer, unless the modem uses adaptive queue management, which the document calls uncommon. The result is delay on the order of seconds, with disastrous effects on application performance. On a cable system with shared capacity between neighbours, one neighbour can saturate the buffer and affect another neighbour's latency, and even users with dedicated bandwidth see delays as their own peer-to-peer traffic saturates the link and dominates their own more latency-sensitive traffic. One approach is for clients to implement congestion control that keeps the bottleneck full while yielding to keep the delay of competing traffic low. Such an algorithm has been implemented in BitTorrent's client by continuously sampling one-way delay, separating propagation delay from queuing delay, and targeting a small queuing delay value, which approximates a scavenger service class by forcing bulk, elastic traffic to yield to competitors under congestion. The P4P framework supports a component that lets applications mark traffic as bulk data and adjust their behaviour to the feedback they receive.

Weighted congestion control would allow hosts to give more weight to interactive applications during congestion. Compared with Diffserv, it could be implemented on hosts with a simple extension to socket APIs, though agreement among operating systems would be needed for portability. Control would sit with the host, whereas with Diffserv it is difficult for a host to know the network is complying with its classifications. Hosts would need some disincentive to set their weights at maximum, whereas Diffserv was not designed for individual users to employ. Both approaches rely on traffic senders to set policies, so congestion arising from peer-to-peer use on the receiver side is not helped by either. The document lists the characteristics of useful approaches: full user control of priorities within the user's own scope, and no possibility of interpreting provider behaviour as discriminatory. One metric that meets these criteria is a harm or cost metric in which cost equals the amount of data that was not served to its destination, so cost is greatest when traffic peaks are greatest. That allows a policy of not sending too much data during congestion without saying exactly how much is too much. One important limitation for providers is that they have no window into congestion on other providers' networks, so solving that needs a separate mechanism to express congestion across domains.

On quality of service, the document notes that providers have tried short-term measures such as using deep packet inspection to change delivery characteristics of certain traffic at times of congestion, which can be more cost effective than adding bandwidth but could lead to a game of measures in which application providers adapt to avoid correct classification. A standardised mechanism that may help is the Differentiated Services Code Points described in RFC 2474. With DSCP, devices at the edge of the network mark packets with the service level they should receive, nodes inside the network need not remember anything about service flows, and applications do not need to request a service level. Its most relevant use for this problem may be usage-based charging, since pricing that charges a premium for real-time traffic could shape behaviour and reduce congestion, and DSCP could also limit a user's supply of high-priority bandwidth. Equipment supporting DSCP is already available and it is widely used by enterprise customers, but it still faces deployment hurdles, the largest of which is the lack of uniform code points across networks, and providers have no means of verifying each other's markings.

A related discussion covered applications that open multiple TCP connections. With several users sharing one link, fairness measured per flow rather than per user gives users with more open connections a larger share of bandwidth. Some peer-to-peer protocols use multiple connections for a single file transfer, and users often run several transfers at once, so a peer-to-peer user can have far more open connections than other users on the same link. A single user with several connections is not a problem on its face, but the fact that fairness is decided per flow rather than per user leaves that impression, and participants thought the IETF might usefully publish information about such situations.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas were put forward for the transport side. A bulk transfer could watch its own delay and slow down when the link is busy, so that a voice call is not delayed. Or the sending program could mark its traffic as bulk, and let the network decide how to treat it, the way the differentiated services code points already do.

sections.title: Work Items and Next Steps
sections.content:
At the conclusion of the workshop and in the days after it, the largest areas of interest fell into two categories: transport issues and improved peer selection. Two transport-related work items evolved. The first was a standardised, delay-based, end-to-end congestion control mechanism that applications such as peer-to-peer clients could use to reduce their own impact on interactive applications on shared links. The second was an informational document describing the current practice of peer-to-peer applications opening multiple transport connections, with recommendations about best practice.

Participants expressed strong interest in pursuing the range of concepts that support information sharing between networks and applications to improve peer selection, with the added appeal of possible use by applications other than peer-to-peer. Because the scope of the solutions discussed was broad, extracting the most feasible pieces to pursue is the necessary first step. The document lists the candidate work items in peer selection: a standard, easier way for clients to obtain autonomous system numbers, since clients currently rely on their own tables; a standardised format for requests and responses to a service that expresses a provider's peering preferences, with the focus on the communication rather than the criteria; a way to discover local trackers, iTrackers, oracles or caches, potentially by leveraging an existing discovery protocol such as DNS, DHCP or anycast; a standard way to communicate a subscriber's current usage status where quotas apply, which would require support for very different provider business models; and a standard tracker format for redirecting from a global tracker to a local one, which the document notes may have an analogue in the indexes of mirror information that HTTP servers build for themselves.

On costs and congestion, participants expressed diverging opinions about how much the cost of transferring data, as experienced by providers and their subscribers, should factor into IETF thinking. Some estimates put the total cost of shipping 1 GB between $0.10 and $2, and the cost of transit bandwidth in markets where subscribers pay flat rates appears to have levelled off. That may lead more providers to move to volume-based pricing, which is only feasible if bandwidth consumption is visible to end users, which argues for a mechanism exposing quotas and usage to applications, though expressing cost information may be outside the technical purview of the IETF. Others saw congestion as merely a manifestation of cost: an ISP that invests in capacity could be seen as paying to relieve congestion, and if subscribers are charged for congesting the network then cost and congestion are one and the same. Participants felt these issues might be useful material for IRTF work.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop ended with a short list. On the transport side, a deferential congestion control for bulk transfers and a note about applications that open many connections. On the peer side, ways for clients to learn which network a peer is in, and for providers to say which peers they would rather connect to.

items.title: Autonomous system numbers
items.text: A standard, easier way for clients to get the mapping they now keep in their own tables.

items.title: Querying for preferred peers
items.text: A standard format for asking a service that knows a provider's peering preferences.

items.title: Resource discovery
items.text: A way to find the local tracker, iTracker, oracle or cache, perhaps using DNS, DHCP or anycast.

items.title: Account usage information
items.text: A standard way to tell a subscriber's application how much of the quota is left.

items.title: Tracker formats
items.text: A standard format for redirecting a query from a global tracker to a local one.
